title: Loops, ranges, comprehensions and scope
outcome: Trace finite iteration and scope rules while using explicit empty-input and indexing policies.
key_terms: A lazy arithmetic sequence such as `1:n` that stores its start, step and stop instead of every element.
Bracketed loop syntax such as `[x^2 for x in xs]` that eagerly builds a new array from an iteration.
Parenthesized loop syntax such as `(x^2 for x in xs)` that produces values on demand, so a reduction needs no intermediate array.
The rule governing assignment to a global name inside a top-level loop, which behaves differently in a script file than in the REPL.
Variables assigned inside a function body are local to each call, which keeps an accumulator free of global ambiguity.
approach: Trace every loop by its iterable. Ranges such as `1:3` include both endpoints, `1:0` is empty, and a descending range needs a negative step. `sum_range` starts its accumulator at 0, so its empty result is 0. Positions come from `eachindex` or `enumerate`, and accumulation lives inside a function so its state is local.

exercises.title: Count an inclusive range
exercises.answer: Inclusive syntax must match the intended number of observations.
exercises.why: `1:3` includes both endpoints, so it holds three values: 1, 2 and 3.
exercises.wrong: Expecting Python-like half-open ranges predicts two values and leaves the last observation out of every loop.
exercises.verify: Check `collect(1:3) == [1, 2, 3]` and `length(1:3) == 3`, the latter already in the reference.

exercises.title: Use zero iterations
exercises.expected: The result is its initial zero.
exercises.hint: An empty iterable performs no loop body.
exercises.answer: The accumulator policy determines the empty-input result; other algorithms may need to reject emptiness.
exercises.why: `1:0` is empty, so the loop body in `sum_range` never runs and `total` keeps its starting value 0.
exercises.wrong: Assuming every loop runs at least once predicts an error or a garbage value, when the accumulator simply returns its initial state.
exercises.verify: Assert `sum_range(1:0) == 0` and `[i for i = 1:0] == Int[]`, which the reference also checks.

exercises.title: Descend explicitly
exercises.task: Construct the descending sequence 3, 2, 1 as a range.
exercises.answer: A positive default step does not produce the requested descending traversal.
exercises.why: `3:-1:1` starts at 3 and adds -1 until it passes 1, giving 3, 2 and 1.
exercises.wrong: Writing `3:1` produces an empty range, because the default step is +1 and 3 is already past the stop.

exercises.title: Keep identity separate
exercises.expected: Positions are 1 and 2; values remain 10 and 20.
exercises.hint: Do not use a data value as an array index accidentally.
exercises.answer: Record identity, position and measurement are distinct roles.
exercises.why: `enumerate([10, 20])` yields pairs `(1, 10)` and `(2, 20)`, keeping positions separate from measured values.
exercises.wrong: Indexing with the values, as in `v[10]`, treats a measurement as a position and throws `BoundsError` on a two-element vector.
exercises.verify: Collect `enumerate([10, 20])` and compare it with `[(1, 10), (2, 20)]`; the reference checks `eachindex([4, 5])` gives 1 and 2.

exercises.title: Avoid an unnecessary collection
exercises.task: Compute only the sum of selected squares.
exercises.expected: A generator can supply the reduction directly.
exercises.hint: Ask whether the intermediate array is needed later.
exercises.answer: This changes materialization, but performance claims still need a measured workload.
exercises.why: `sum(i^2 for i in 1:3 if isodd(i))` feeds 1 and 9 directly to `sum`, giving 10 without allocating an intermediate array.
exercises.wrong: Claiming the generator is faster without timing assumes allocation dominates, which this tiny input cannot show either way.
exercises.verify: Assert the generator sum equals `sum([i^2 for i in 1:3 if isodd(i)])`; the reference checks `sum(i for i = 1:3) == 6`.

exercises.title: Trace scope
exercises.task: Move a reusable accumulation into a function with explicit input.
exercises.expected: Its local state is recreated on every call.
exercises.hint: Compare the function boundary with ambient script globals.
exercises.answer: Explicit inputs and outputs make both reasoning and runtime specialization easier to inspect.
exercises.why: Inside `sum_range`, `total = 0` runs on every call, so `sum_range(-2:2)` gives 0 and `sum_range(2:2)` gives 2 independently.
exercises.wrong: Updating a top-level `total` inside a script's `for` loop triggers the soft-scope ambiguity warning and then an undefined-variable error.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `sum_range(2:2) == 2` and `sum_range(-2:2) == 0`; call them in either order and expect the same results.

checks_note: Each assertion covers a boundary of a counting loop. `sum_range(2:2)` has exactly one element, `-2:2` cancels to zero, and `1:0` is empty so the comprehension yields `Int[]`. `sum(i for i = 1:3) == 6` checks a generator without building an array, and `eachindex([4, 5])` returns the positions 1 and 2, not the stored values 4 and 5. A loop that started at zero would break the length check.
